paras: The lynching of John Fogle took place early on November 28, 1903, near Ross, a small railway station in Dorchester County, South Carolina, when a mob hanged and shot a Black man of about thirty accused of attempting to assault a young white woman. Hunted overnight with bloodhounds, Fogle was taken before his accuser for identification and then strung to a tree and shot. The Associated Press reported it as the first lynching in the county's history, the angle many headlines took.

Ross (also Rosses, Rose's or Ross' Station) stood on the Southern Railway thirty-seven miles from Charleston by the AP's count, and between eight and twelve miles from St. George, the town from which the local correspondents wrote. According to the St. George correspondents, a young woman living about three miles from Ross was attacked on the afternoon of Friday, November 27, and fought off her attacker, who left her choked and bruised. A Charleston dispatch sent before any capture gave a different version, naming her as Miss Way, aged 16, and saying an "unknown negro" had forced his way into her room at 11 o'clock that night.

As word spread, a posse left St. George for Ross. By nightfall, The State's correspondent wrote, "a mob aggregating 200 or 300 men from the adjacent towns and country, bent upon vengeance" had gathered there. Bloodhounds belonging to a Mr. Burton of Charleston arrived on the midnight train and were put on the trail at 1:30 in the morning. Accounts of the capture differ: a Columbia dispatch said the dogs traced Fogle to his cabin, while the AP said he had fled to the swamps and was found there.

The AP reported that Fogle was "seized by the mob before the sheriff could interfere" and carried before the woman, who identified him. The mob, taking the woman along according to The State, then went into the woods near a swamp, where he was hanged from the limb of a tree and his body was shot through. The Keowee Courier's version had the body riddled "with bullets from a hundred guns," and The State reported that it was left hanging there.
No report of an inquest, an arrest or any official inquiry into the lynching appears in the coverage, and no member of the mob was named.

The story moved first as a Charleston wire predicting that "the black brute, if caught, will be lynched," then as an Associated Press report that ran on November 29 in Richmond, New York, Savannah and Birmingham. Its headlines stressed the broken county record, with the New-York Tribune heading it "A GOOD RECORD GONE," and they stated the assault as fact; the Fredericksburg Free Lance was the exception with "Negro Accused Of Assault Hanged And Then Shot." Through early December the case shrank to one-line items in digest columns from Illinois to Maryland, which gave the accuser's name variously as Rose, Ross or Way and the victim's as Fogle or Fagle.

South Carolina weeklies, reprinting the Columbia State and the Charleston News and Courier, went further in endorsing the mob. The Bamberg Herald ran The State's dispatch as "A NEGRO BRUTE LYNCHED," calling Fogle a "rape fiend" and lamenting that "Another white home has been despoiled," while the Lancaster Enterprise headed the same text "Citizens Take Law in Their Own Hands." The News and Courier's St. George correspondent closed by calling the lynching "the only remedy" taken "by this crowd of determined men."

The only Black-press notice found was a single line in the Richmond Planet's weekly digest of December 5, which reported that John Fagle was lynched at Ross Station and, unlike most white headlines, described the accusation as a charge, without comment.

The papers disagreed on the man's name, printed Fogle by the South Carolina correspondents and Fagle in some AP copies and in the Planet. The accuser was unnamed in the local reports, while wire briefs called her Miss Way, Miss Rose or Miss Ross, the last two matching the name of the station. The time of the alleged attack ranged from 3 o'clock in the afternoon in The State's account to 11 o'clock at night in the earliest Charleston wire.

reader.title: Lynching of John Fogle
bases: A Black man accused of attempted assault was hunted with bloodhounds by a crowd of armed men, hanged from a tree and shot, with no legal proceeding (A3, A4, A18).

Every account says Fogle was hanged and shot by a 'mob' (A3, A4) that The State's correspondent put at 200 or 300 men (A18), seized 'before the sheriff could interfere' (A4), as punishment for an alleged attempted assault on a white woman (A18, A17).

Independent dispatches from the Associated Press at Charleston (A4), a Columbia correspondent (A3), the News and Courier's St. George correspondent (A17) and The State's St. George correspondent (A18) agree on the hunt, the identification and the hanging and shooting.

accounts.label: Associated Press (Charleston)
accounts.gist: Fogle attempted an assault at the woman's home near Ross' Station 'last night', fled to the swamps, was trailed by Charleston bloodhounds, seized by the mob before the sheriff could interfere, identified, hanged and shot.

accounts.label: Early Charleston wire (before capture)
accounts.gist: Miss Way, 16, was assaulted at 11 p.m. by an unknown man who forced his way into her room; an armed posse with bloodhounds was out and he would be lynched if caught.

accounts.label: The State's St. George correspondent
accounts.gist: The alleged attempt was at 3 p.m.; a posse left St. George and a mob of 200 or 300 gathered; hounds found Fogle at 1:30 a.m. or later; the mob took him and the woman to woods near a swamp and left his body hanging.

accounts.label: News and Courier's St. George correspondent
accounts.gist: The woman lived three miles from Rosses; Mr. Burton's hounds came on the midnight train; Fogle was caught, identified and hanged and shot by 'this crowd of determined men', whose act the writer endorsed.

accounts.label: Black press digest
accounts.gist: A one-line item: John Fagle, 'Charged with an attempted criminal assault', was lynched at Ross Station.

framing.detail: South Carolina weeklies headed it 'A NEGRO BRUTE LYNCHED' and 'Citizens Take Law in Their Own Hands', called Fogle a 'rape fiend' and 'the perpetrator of the heinous crime', and the News and Courier letter called the lynching 'the only remedy'.

Northern and Southern dailies ran the AP text as a record broken ('A GOOD RECORD GONE.', 'FIRST LYNCHING IN DORCHESTER'), stating the assault as fact; the Free Lance alone headed it 'Negro Accused Of Assault'.
Digest columns in Illinois, Kentucky and Maryland reduced it to one line naming the charge.
The Richmond Planet carried one line in its weekly news digest, framing the charge as a charge ('Charged with an attempted criminal assault'), with no comment.

Rose and Ross match the station's name and may be confusions with it; the local correspondents do not name her.

St. George is the dateline; the alleged assault and the lynching were at or near Ross (Rosses, Ross' Station), 8 to 12 miles from St. George

Also hanging from a tree and shooting the body; identification before the accuser
A posse left St. George, but every account calls the killers a 'mob' or 'crowd' of 200 or 300 men; no legal deputization is reported
